strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: directly tokenizing raw SMPL/3D motion sequences instead of relying on 2D-rendered pose images, which is a promising alternative for human image animation.
The proposed framework is technically coherent: 4DMoT quantizes SMPL motion into discrete motion tokens, and MV-DiT integrates them via 4D motion attention, 4D RoPE, and motion-aware CFG.
Strong headline quantitative results on TikTok, especially FID-VID (6.98) and FID (19.46), with substantial improvements over many prior methods.
Ablation studies provide useful evidence for the importance of vector quantization and the proposed positional encoding design, including codebook usage analysis and visualizations.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: anonymous code link, detailed architecture/training hyperparameters, dataset curation pipeline, training curves, and limitations/ethics discussion are included.
Qualitative results demonstrate impressive identity preservation and generalization to diverse artistic styles, characters, and scenarios.
weaknesses: The central claim that 4D motion tokens outperform 2D-rendered pose images is not directly tested under a controlled setting: there is no ablation replacing 4DMoT with 2D pose/SMPL renderings while keeping the same MV-DiT, base model, and training data. The comparison to prior methods confounds representation choice with architecture, training data, and model scale.

Evaluation is limited to the TikTok benchmark with only a few test sequences, while open-world generalization is supported mainly by qualitative examples. Quantitative evaluation on unseen domains, multiple characters, and diverse styles is missing.

There is a direct inconsistency between the abstract/introduction, which claims generalization to multiple characters, and Appendix B, which states that the current version cannot support multi-person animations with different poses.

The novelty is somewhat overstated: prior human animation methods already use 3D/SMPL guidance, and motion tokenization is adapted from existing motion-generation works. The specific contribution is the integration into a DiT-based animation pipeline, but the framing as a completely new paradigm is stronger than the evidence justifies.

The 4D RoPE spatial component appears to use dataset-averaged joint positions rather than per-frame dynamic 3D joint positions, so it may primarily encode joint identity/static skeleton structure rather than true dynamic 4D spatial motion.
Some metrics are not uniformly better: PSNR and SSIM are lower than Human-DiT, and FVD is only slightly better than Animate Anyone 2 (140.60 vs. 144.65), so the advantage is metric-dependent.

Details and reproducibility of the curated 5K training dataset are limited: it combines public, web-crawled, and AI-generated videos, but the dataset is not released and potential overlap with TikTok evaluation sequences is not clarified.
Missing ablations on the reference-image concatenation strategy and the design of the learnable unconditional motion tokens make it difficult to attribute gains to all claimed components.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging task: open-world pose-guided human image animation.
Proposes a potentially interesting direction: bypassing 2D-rendered pose images and directly conditioning a video DiT on tokenized SMPL/3D joint motion.
The overall pipeline is clearly described, with a motion VQVAE, motion-aware DiT, 4D motion attention, and motion-aware CFG.
Provides code/demo links and implementation details, which improves reproducibility relative to many works in this area.
Includes ablation studies over quantization, positional encoding choices, and CFG scale, as well as codebook utilization analysis.
Reports a large improvement in FID-VID on TikTok, which is a striking result if it holds under controlled evaluation.
Qualitative results show appealing generalization to anime, ink, pixel-art, and photorealistic characters.
Includes a limitations and ethics discussion.
weaknesses: The central claim—that directly modeling 4D motion tokens is better than 2D-rendered pose guidance—is not directly validated. The paper lacks a controlled baseline that replaces 4D motion attention with a 2D pose/SMPL-rendering condition under the same base model, training data, and compute.

The main comparisons are heavily confounded. MTVCrafter uses a 7B-parameter CogVideoX-5B pretrained video DiT and a curated 5K-clip dataset, while baselines differ in base model, pretraining, training data, and compute. The reported gains may reflect these factors rather than 4D motion tokenization.

Evaluation is limited to TikTok sequences 335–340, i.e., only six test videos, with no confidence intervals or statistical significance. FID-VID 6.98 on such a small set may be high-variance, and the FVD gain over the second-best is small.

The paper overclaims SOTA across all metrics, but PSNR and SSIM are worse than several baselines (e.g., UniAnimate, Human-DiT, Champ). The text later dismisses PSNR/SSIM as less significant, which is not sufficient to support the initial claim.

The claim of handling single or multiple characters is contradicted by Appendix B, which states the method cannot support multi-person animations with different poses. This is a serious overclaim in the abstract, contribution list, and Figure 1.

The 4D RoPE design is technically questionable. Cross-attention between vision tokens with 3D RoPE (t,h,w) and motion tokens with 4D RoPE (t,x,y,z) has no clear relative-position interpretation because the two spaces and dimensional splits differ.

The spatial component of the 4D RoPE is computed from dataset-mean joint positions rather than per-frame actual joint coordinates. It therefore encodes static joint identity/average skeleton layout, not the actual dynamic 3D spatial relationships the paper claims to restore after tokenization.

Critical motion-tokenizer details are missing. The codebook size is 8,192 with code dimension 3,072 and roughly 50M parameters, but reconstruction quality is only visualized qualitatively; no MPJPE/acceleration/jitter metrics are reported.

Dataset curation may introduce contamination or bias. The 5K clips are collected from public/web/AI-generated sources without explicitly excluding TikTok test sequences, and the curated dataset is not released, limiting reproducibility.

Baseline comparison is incomplete and unfair: several methods lack all metrics, some numbers are taken from original papers under different settings, and no effort is made to equalize base models, training data, or training compute.

Robustness to pose estimation failures is not evaluated. The method depends on NLF-Pose SMPL estimation, but training filters out high-uncertainty poses and the paper does not test noisy, missing, or half-body pose inputs at inference.
Open-world generalization is demonstrated only qualitatively. There is no quantitative open-world benchmark or user study, so the broad claims of robust open-world animation remain unsupported.
The method admits failures on non-human anatomy and precise hand articulation, which are central to the claimed open-world setting, but these failures are not quantified or addressed technically.
Ethical/copyright concerns around animating copyrighted characters and identities are acknowledged but not resolved; safeguards are only planned.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated direction for human image animation by directly tokenizing raw 4D motion (SMPL joint sequences) rather than relying on 2D-rendered pose images, avoiding pixel-level pose-image alignment and preserving richer spatio-temporal cues.

The proposed 4DMoT is a reasonable adaptation of VQ-VAE tokenization to motion sequences, with codebook utilization analysis and reconstruction evaluations on unseen gymnastics data supporting its effectiveness.

MV-DiT integrates 4D motion attention, 4D RoPE, motion-aware CFG, and reference-image concatenation into a strong CogVideoX-based DiT backbone, and the overall system produces high-quality qualitative results across diverse styles and characters.

Reports state-of-the-art results on the TikTok benchmark, with especially strong FID-VID improvement (6.98 vs. second-best ~20.64) and competitive FVD, supported by qualitative comparisons against several recent baselines.
Includes useful ablation studies on motion token quantization, positional encoding choices, and CFG scale, as well as dataset curation and implementation details in the appendix.
Provides anonymous code/demos and discusses limitations and misuse risks, which is a positive step for reproducibility and responsible research.
weaknesses: The central claim that 4D motion tokens are superior to 2D-rendered pose guidance is not fully isolated experimentally: there is no controlled comparison using the same MV-DiT architecture, training data, and compute budget with 2D rendered SMPL/depth/skeleton conditions.

The quantitative evaluation is narrow, relying only on the TikTok dataset. No other standard human animation benchmark (e.g., Fashion, UBC) is used, and there are no pose/motion-accuracy metrics (e.g., PCK/MPJPE) despite motion fidelity being a core claim.

The multi-person claim is inconsistent: the abstract/introduction/figures advertise multiple characters, but Appendix B states that the current model cannot support multi-person animations with different poses. This overclaims open-world capability.

The 4D RoPE design is somewhat questionable: spatial coordinates are based on dataset-wide mean joint positions rather than per-frame actual joint coordinates, so the positional encoding mainly provides canonical joint identity/time cues rather than true 4D spatial motion. The cross-modal RoPE between vision and motion tokens is also not clearly justified.

Ablations are insufficient for the strongest claims: there is no ablation of reference concatenation vs. ReferenceNet-style preservation, no comparison of 4D motion tokens vs. rendered pose images inside the same DiT, and no analysis of codebook size, token count, or training-data scale.

Evaluation protocol and baseline fairness are not fully convincing. Baselines differ substantially in base architecture, training data, compute, and resolution, and some baseline numbers are missing or taken from original papers; the large FID-VID gap is not explained relative to the much smaller FVD gap.

Reproducibility is limited because the curated 5K motion-video dataset, including web-crawled and AI-generated sources, is not released, and the method depends on an external SMPL estimator whose failures may propagate to open-world settings.

Ethical/data concerns around web-crawled videos, AI-generated content, copyright, and consent are acknowledged but not resolved; planned safeguards such as watermarking/consent verification are not implemented or evaluated.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel motion representation for character animation: directly tokenizing temporally evolving SMPL joint coordinates instead of using 2D-rendered pose images, which helps decouple motion from appearance and absolute position.

The proposed 4DMoT is technically reasonable and well-supported: it uses a VQVAE-style discrete tokenizer over differential joint coordinates, with codebook utilization and reconstruction analyses, and ablations over quantization and differential motion.

The MV-DiT design is coherent: 4D motion attention with motion-aware CFG and 4D positional encodings is integrated into DiT backbones, and the framework scales from approximately 6B to 18B parameters, demonstrating practical scalability.

Empirical results are strong on the TikTok and Fashion benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive scores on most metrics, with extensive qualitative comparisons and ablations on key components.

The paper demonstrates impressive qualitative zero-shot generalization to diverse characters, styles, half-body/full-body settings, and even non-human subjects, showing the potential impact of the motion-token representation.
weaknesses: The claim that the method directly models 'raw 3D motion' or '4D motion' is somewhat overstated: the pipeline still relies on SMPL parameter estimation from RGB videos, so it is not raw sensor-level 4D motion and inherits pose-estimation errors and biases.

Open-world generalization to non-human subjects, animals, and objects is shown mainly qualitatively. There is no dedicated quantitative benchmark or user study for these cases, so the strength of the zero-shot claim is not fully measured.

Evaluation is limited to two relatively old benchmarks, TikTok and Fashion, which are mostly human dance/fashion videos. The paper lacks evaluation on newer, larger, and more diverse character-animation benchmarks, and some recent 3D/SMPL-based baselines are not compared.

The 4D RoPE for motion tokens uses dataset-averaged joint positions rather than per-frame/per-token dynamic 3D coordinates. Although this design is ablated, it is not genuinely a full 4D positional encoding of each motion token and may limit fine-grained spatial motion specificity.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: training data is web-crawled and not released, code/checkpoints are promised but not fully available in the submission, and dataset consent/privacy issues around human videos are acknowledged but not concretely resolved.

Several architectural choices, such as inserting motion attention every two blocks, the repeat-and-concatenate identity scheme, and zero-padding for the 18B model, are not ablated or analyzed in depth. Inference cost and deployment details are also limited.

There are minor inconsistencies and presentation issues: the 6B model is described as based on CogVideoX-5B, some baseline citations/table entries appear ambiguous, and MTVCraft is not best on every metric (e.g., LPIPS on Fashion).

strengths: Introduces a framework that conditions video diffusion on tokenized SMPL joint sequences instead of rendered pose images, potentially reducing shape/position biases and enabling more flexible control.
Combines a motion tokenizer (4DMoT) with a motion-aware video DiT (MV-DiT) and 4D positional encodings, and demonstrates scalability to 6B and 18B backbones.
Reports strong quantitative results on TikTok and Fashion benchmarks, with notable improvements in FID/FVD/FID-VID over several prior methods.
Qualitative results show impressive generalization to diverse styles, non-human subjects, and open-world characters.
weaknesses: The central claim—that direct 4D motion tokens are superior to 2D pose images—is not directly validated with a controlled baseline using the same DiT backbone and training setup but 2D pose renderings. Existing comparisons confound architecture, base model size, and training data.

State-of-the-art comparisons are confounded by model scale and data: MTVCraft-18B uses Wan-2.1-14B, much larger than most baselines, and is trained on a large curated dataset. No comparison to similarly scaled pose-guided baselines is provided.

The '4D RoPE' for motion tokens uses dataset-averaged mean joint positions rather than actual per-token spatial coordinates, so the spatial component is essentially a constant joint-type embedding; this weakens the 4D positional encoding claim.

Missing quantitative evaluation of 4DMoT reconstruction quality (e.g., MPJPE, acceleration error). Ablation evidence is limited, with small differences and no error bars or statistical significance tests.
Reproducibility concerns: the curated 30K/200K web-crawled dataset is not released, project/code links are incomplete, and reproducing the 18B model training is likely difficult.
Inconsistency about text conditioning: the 6B model reportedly removes the text branch, but evaluation details mention text prompts and a text CFG scale.
Zero-shot generalization claims are supported mainly by qualitative examples; no quantitative zero-shot protocol or user study is provided.
Ethical concerns are under-addressed: training on web-crawled human data, potential identity manipulation, and commercial deployment without detailed consent/watermarking safeguards.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated and novel direction for pose-guided character animation: directly tokenizing 4D motion (3D joint coordinates over time) instead of relying on 2D-rendered pose images. This addresses two clear limitations of prior work—discarded spatial-temporal information and pixel-level pose copying—and the motivation is convincingly illustrated.

The technical design is coherent and substantial. 4DMoT introduces a VQ-VAE over differential SMPL joint coordinates with quantization, EMA codebook updates, and codebook resetting. MV-DiT then injects 4D motion attention and 4D RoPE into a video DiT, enabling motion tokens to act as context for video generation. The motion-aware CFG and scalability to 6B/18B scales further strengthen the framework.

Empirical evaluation is strong. MTVCraft achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive results on the TikTok and Fashion benchmarks across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, FVD, and FID-VID. The ablation studies validate key choices, including discrete quantization, differential motion, z-axis quantization, and 4D positional encoding designs.

The qualitative results demonstrate impressive generalization to diverse styles, full-body/half-body characters, non-human subjects, and open-world scenarios. The paper also includes extensive implementation details, dataset curation details, training details, ethical discussion, and claimed code release, which support reproducibility and practical impact.
weaknesses: The comparison against baselines may not be fully controlled. MTVCraft-18B uses a large Wan-2.1-14B backbone and a curated 30K high-quality motion-video dataset, while several baselines use smaller or different backbones and likely less data. A same-backbone, same-data comparison against a 2D-rendered pose-image conditioning baseline would better isolate the contribution of the proposed 4D motion tokenization.

The central claims about zero-shot generalization to arbitrary characters, styles, and non-human objects are supported mainly by qualitative figures. There is no quantitative zero-shot benchmark, user study, or systematic evaluation on unseen non-human categories, so it is difficult to rule out that part of the generalization comes from the strong base generative models rather than the motion tokenization.

The 4D RoPE design uses dataset-averaged joint positions for the spatial coordinates of motion tokens, rather than per-frame joint positions. This means the spatial part of the positional encoding is largely fixed anatomical indexing rather than true per-frame 3D geometry. While ablations show it works better than alternatives, the claimed 4D spatial-temporal encoding may not fully capture dynamic 3D structure.

The data pipeline relies on NLF-Pose and a standard neutral SMPL shape, which can introduce pose estimation errors and may discard actor-specific body proportions and physical constraints such as contact. The paper acknowledges weak hand articulation, but broader physical plausibility and motion retargeting fidelity are not quantitatively evaluated.

Some claims are overstated. Terms such as “first” and “raw 4D motion” should be qualified, since the method uses estimated SMPL parameters, a standard skeleton, and differential joint coordinates rather than unprocessed motion. The relation to prior 3D parametric guidance methods is discussed but not fully isolated experimentally.

The paper contains some citation and baseline-table inconsistencies, e.g., MusePose and MooraAA both cited as Hu (2024), and some metrics are re-evaluated while others are taken from prior papers. These issues do not invalidate the results but weaken evaluation clarity and reproducibility.
